comment: Example client configs for laptops on the same LAN. Replace 'your-mac.local' with your host's mDNS name or LAN IP. The domestic template serves SIX lanes from one endpoint: 'heavy' + 'medium' + 'flash' + 'super-flash' (cloud) and 'local-orch' + 'local-sub' (host GPU). A lane name is the stable contract - the host can swap the model behind it without any client edit. Point the main model at a driving lane ('heavy' or 'local-orch') and the worker/subagent model at its cheap partner ('flash', 'super-flash', or 'local-sub'). Select 'medium' explicitly for substantive coding or review work; it does not change the default driver, worker, or housekeeping roles. Client bootstrap also installs `opencode-cloud`, `opencode-local`, and `opencode-super` profiles. Easiest of all: just run `ferry opencode` on the client to write the opencode block below automatically. Every generated config also carries a fleet-identity `headers` map under `options` — `X-Ferry-Client` (this machine's name) and `X-Ferry-Fleet` (from `$FERRY_FLEET`, for a one-shot pin) — which `ferry opencode` / `ferry claude` write for you; see the `options` block below for the shape. Since fleets (2026-09-04) the host may run several complete routing sets behind these same bare lane names at once; which one you get depends on 'X-Ferry-Fleet', your sticky selection, or the host default — see README.md's Fleets section.

opencode._tip: Or just run `ferry opencode` on the client to write this automatically.

generic_openai_sdk_python.code:
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url='http://your-mac.local:8090/v1',
    api_key='local'
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model='heavy',
    messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': 'Tell me a joke.'}]
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
